questions.title: A quadratic whose second root the sum to infinity forbids
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 1.8 (sum of infinite convergent geometric sequences) and SL 1.3 (geometric sequences and series)
questions.subtopic: 1.8 Sum of infinite convergent geometric sequences and 1.3 Geometric sequences and series
questions.challenge_mechanism: The lever is that the quadratic produced by the given data has two legitimate roots, and only the convergence condition decides which one the series can actually use.
questions.question: A geometric series has second term $-6$ and sum to infinity $8$. Its first term is $a$ and its common ratio is $r$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that the second term is $-6$ and the sum to infinity is $8$, show that $4r^2 - 4r - 3 = 0$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the two possible values of the common ratio $r$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine which of these two values of $r$ is admissible for a convergent series, and find the corresponding first term $a$ and third term $ar^2$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the sum of the first ten terms of the convergent series, giving your answer as an exact fraction.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The second term is $ar = -6$, so $a = -6/r$. **(M1)** The two relations $ar = -6$ and $a/(1-r) = 8$ are the only information available, so eliminating $a$ is the natural first move. Substituting this into the sum to infinity $a/(1-r) = 8$ gives $-6/r = 8(1-r)$, so $-6 = 8r(1-r)$. **(M1)** Expanding the right-hand side, $-6 = 8r - 8r^2$, and bringing every term to one side gives $8r^2 - 8r - 6 = 0$. **(A1)** Dividing through by $2$ yields $4r^2 - 4r - 3 = 0$, as required. **(AG)**

**(b)** Factorising, $4r^2 - 4r - 3 = (2r - 3)(2r + 1)$. **(M1)** Setting each factor to zero gives $2r - 3 = 0$ or $2r + 1 = 0$, so $r = 3/2$ or $r = -1/2$. **(A1)** Both values satisfy the quadratic, which substitution confirms. **(A1)**

**(c)** A geometric series converges to a finite sum only when $|r| < 1$. **(R1)** For $r = 3/2$ we have $|r| = 1.5 > 1$, so this series diverges and cannot have sum to infinity $8$; that root must be rejected. **(R1)** For $r = -1/2$ we have $|r| = 0.5 < 1$, so this is the admissible value. **(A1)** Then $a = -6/(-1/2) = 12$, and the third term is $ar^2 = 12(1/4) = 3$. **(A1)** Checking the sum, $12/(1 - (-1/2)) = 12/(3/2) = 8$, as required. **(A1)**

**(d)** The sum of the first $n$ terms is $S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)$. **(M1)** With $a = 12$, $r = -1/2$ and $n = 10$, this is $S_{10} = 12(1 - (-1/2)^{10})/(1 + 1/2)$. **(M1)** Now $(-1/2)^{10} = 1/1024$ and $1 + 1/2 = 3/2$, so $S_{10} = 12(1023/1024)/(3/2) = 8(1023/1024)$. **(A1)** Hence $S_{10} = 8184/1024 = 1023/128$. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: Part (a) carries two **(M1)** marks: the first is for translating the second term into $ar = -6$ and hence $a = -6/r$, and the second is for substituting that expression into the sum-to-infinity formula. The **(A1)** is for reaching $8r^2 - 8r - 6 = 0$ in a correct unsimplified form, and the **(AG)** confirms the printed answer, so a candidate who simply quotes $4r^2 - 4r - 3 = 0$ without the substitution earns nothing. In part (b) the **(M1)** is for a valid factorisation or for applying the quadratic formula, and the two **(A1)** marks are for the two roots; a candidate who finds only $r = 3/2$ loses the second **(A1)**. Part (c) is the discriminating part: the first **(R1)** is for stating the convergence condition $|r| < 1$, the second **(R1)** is for rejecting $r = 3/2$ because $|3/2| > 1$ even though it satisfies the quadratic, and the three **(A1)** marks are for the admissible ratio, the first term $a = 12$ and the third term $ar^2 = 3$. Part (d) awards **(M1)** for quoting the finite-sum formula, **(M1)** for the substitution, and **(A1)(A1)** for the simplification and the exact fraction $1023/128$; a decimal such as $7.99$ loses the final **(A1)** because the question demands an exact fraction.
questions.explanation:
The item is built so that the algebra of part (a) and the convergence condition of part (c) pull in opposite directions. The substitution $ar = -6$ into $a/(1-r) = 8$ is standard, and it produces a quadratic whose two roots are both genuine roots of that quadratic; nothing in the algebra of parts (a) and (b) can tell the candidate which one is wanted. The decisive fact is that a geometric series has a finite sum to infinity only when $|r| < 1$, so the root $r = 3/2$ is a valid solution of the equation but not a valid common ratio for a convergent series. This is the trap: a candidate who stops at part (b) and reports both roots has answered a different question from the one asked.

The negative ratio $r = -1/2$ then has to be carried forward correctly. The first term follows from $a = -6/r = 12$, the third term from $ar^2 = 3$, and the check $12/(1 + 1/2) = 8$ confirms that the reconstructed series really does have the stated sum. Part (d) rewards exactness: the alternating ratio makes $(-1/2)^{10}$ positive, so the finite sum is slightly below $8$, and the exact value is $1023/128$. A candidate who works with decimals will see $7.9921875$ and may not recognise the fraction, which is why the command term insists on an exact fraction. The rejection of the positive root is the whole point of the exercise: an examiner expects the candidate to say explicitly that $|r| > 1$ prevents convergence, not merely to discard the root because it looks large. Both roots solve the quadratic, so the arithmetic alone cannot separate them, and a final check that the surviving series really does sum to $8$ closes the argument.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 1.8 bullet on the sum of infinite convergent geometric sequences and the SL 1.3 bullet on geometric sequences and series. The design gives data that produce a quadratic with two legitimate roots, so the convergence condition, not the algebra, decides which root the series can use. The second term -6, the sum to infinity 8, the roots r = 3/2 and r = -1/2, the admissible first term 12, the third term 3 and the exact fraction 1023/128 are all constructed here, and the rejection of r = 3/2 is the point of the item.

verification.method: Each root was substituted into the quadratic, the first and third terms were recomputed from $a = -6/r$, and the finite sum was evaluated symbolically against the exact fraction.

questions.title: The greatest coefficient, attained twice
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 1.9 (the binomial theorem: expansion of (a + b)^n and the general term)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The lever is that the ratio of consecutive coefficients equals one at a particular index, so the largest coefficient is shared by two adjacent terms rather than held by a single one.
questions.question: In the expansion of $(1 + x/2)^n$, where $n$ is a positive integer, the coefficients of $x^4$ and $x^5$ are equal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Given that the coefficients of $x^4$ and $x^5$ are equal, show that $n = 14$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the greatest coefficient in the expansion, stating the term or terms at which it occurs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence find the coefficient of $x^6$ in the expansion of $(1 + x/2)^{14}(1 - x)^3$.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The general term of the expansion is $\binom{n}{r}(x/2)^r$, so the coefficient of $x^r$ is $\binom{n}{r}/2^r$. **(M1)** Equating the coefficients of $x^4$ and $x^5$ gives $\binom{n}{4}/2^4 = \binom{n}{5}/2^5$. **(M1)** Multiplying by $2^5$ and dividing by $\binom{n}{5}$ gives $\binom{n}{4}/\binom{n}{5} = 1/2$. **(M1)** Now $\binom{n}{4}/\binom{n}{5} = 5/(n-4)$, so $5/(n-4) = 1/2$. **(A1)** Hence $n - 4 = 10$ and $n = 14$, as required. **(AG)**

**(b)** Write $t_r = \binom{14}{r}/2^r$ for the coefficient of $x^r$. **(M1)** The ratio of consecutive coefficients is $t_{r+1}/t_r = (1/2)\binom{14}{r+1}/\binom{14}{r} = (1/2)(14-r)/(r+1)$. **(M1)** This ratio is at least $1$ exactly when $14 - r \ge 2(r+1)$, that is $14 - r \ge 2r + 2$, so $r \le 4$. **(A1)** The coefficients therefore increase up to $r = 4$, and at $r = 4$ the ratio equals $1$, so $t_4 = t_5$; for $r > 4$ the ratio is below $1$ and the coefficients decrease. **(R1)** The greatest coefficient is thus $t_4 = \binom{14}{4}/2^4 = 1001/16 = 62.5625$. **(A1)** It is attained twice, by the terms in $x^4$ and $x^5$, since $t_5 = \binom{14}{5}/2^5 = 2002/32 = 1001/16$. **(A1)** Because the ratio equals exactly $1$ at $r = 4$, the two largest coefficients are equal and every other coefficient is strictly smaller. For comparison, $t_3 = 364/8 = 45.5$ and $t_6 = 3003/64 = 46.921875$, both smaller. **(R1)**

**(c)** Expanding, $(1 - x)^3 = 1 - 3x + 3x^2 - x^3$. **(M1)** If $a_r$ denotes the coefficient of $x^r$ in $(1 + x/2)^{14}$, then the coefficient of $x^6$ in the product is $a_6 - 3a_5 + 3a_4 - a_3$. **(M1)** Substituting, this is $3003/64 - 3(1001/16) + 3(1001/16) - 364/8$. **(A1)** The two middle terms cancel exactly, leaving $3003/64 - 364/8$. **(A1)** Writing over the common denominator $64$, this is $3003/64 - 2912/64 = 91/64$. **(A1)** Hence the coefficient is $91/64 = 1.421875$. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: Part (a) awards **(M1)** for writing the general term $\binom{n}{r}(x/2)^r$, **(M1)** for equating the two coefficients, and **(M1)** for using the ratio $\binom{n}{4}/\binom{n}{5} = 5/(n-4)$; the **(A1)** is for $n - 4 = 10$ and the **(AG)** confirms $n = 14$. A candidate who equates $\binom{n}{4}$ and $\binom{n}{5}$ without the factors $2^4$ and $2^5$ obtains $n = 9$ and loses the **(A1)** and the **(AG)**. In part (b) the **(M1)** marks are for defining $t_r$ and for forming the ratio $t_{r+1}/t_r = (1/2)(14-r)/(r+1)$, and the **(A1)** is for the inequality $r \le 4$. The **(R1)** is for the deduction that the coefficients rise to $r = 4$ and fall afterwards, which forces $t_4 = t_5$; a candidate who merely states a maximum at $r = 4$ without the increase-then-decrease argument loses that mark. The two **(A1)** marks are for the value $1001/16$ and for naming both terms, and the final **(R1)** rewards the numerical comparison with $t_3$ and $t_6$. Part (c) awards **(M1)** for the expansion of $(1-x)^3$ and **(M1)** for the convolution $a_6 - 3a_5 + 3a_4 - a_3$; the **(A1)** marks are for the correct substitution, the exact cancellation of the two middle terms, and the value $91/64$. A candidate who drops the signs on the odd terms obtains a value near $125$, so the signs must be preserved.
questions.explanation:
The stem is a coefficient-matching problem, but the equality of two coefficients is only the entry point; the real work is deciding where the coefficients stop growing. In part (a) the factors $2^r$ from $(x/2)^r$ must be carried into the comparison, and it is the ratio $\binom{n}{4}/\binom{n}{5} = 5/(n-4)$ that reduces the condition to a one-line equation. The common error is to compare binomial coefficients alone, which shifts the answer from $n = 14$ to $n = 9$ and destroys the later parts.

Part (b) turns on the ratio of consecutive coefficients, $t_{r+1}/t_r = (1/2)(14-r)/(r+1)$. The coefficients increase while this ratio exceeds $1$ and decrease once it falls below $1$, and the critical case is when the ratio equals $1$ exactly: that happens at $r = 4$, so the maximum is shared by the terms in $x^4$ and $x^5$. This tie is the twist, because a candidate who assumes a single greatest term will report only one of the two.

Part (c) hides a designed cancellation. Multiplying by $(1-x)^3$ mixes four consecutive coefficients with alternating signs, and because $a_4 = a_5$ the two middle contributions cancel exactly, leaving only $a_6 - a_3$. The result $91/64$ is far smaller than the individual coefficients, which is a strong signal that the cancellation was intended. Truncating the product or mis-signed terms give answers of a completely different size. The candidate is also expected to recognise that the tie at $r = 4$ is exact rather than approximate, because the ratio equals $1$ precisely there; this is why the maximum is shared by two terms and not attained at a single index. Reporting only $t_4$ or only $t_5$ therefore answers only half of the question, and the markscheme requires both to be named explicitly.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 1.9 bullet on the binomial theorem and the general term. The design makes the ratio of consecutive coefficients equal to one at an integer index, so the largest coefficient is shared by two adjacent terms rather than held by a single one. The expansion of (1 + x/2)^n, the equality of the coefficients of x^4 and x^5, the resulting n = 14, the doubled maximum 1001/16, and the closing coefficient 91/64, in which the two middle contributions cancel exactly, are all constructed here.

verification.method: Every binomial coefficient was recomputed in Python, the consecutive-coefficient ratios were checked at the decisive indices, and the cancellation in the product was verified numerically.

questions.title: A family of lines with one member the gradient formula cannot reach
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 2.1 (different forms of the equation of a straight line) and SL 2.4 (determining key features of graphs)
questions.subtopic: 2.1 Different forms of the equation of a straight line and 2.4 Key features of graphs
questions.challenge_mechanism: The lever is that one parameter value makes the coefficient of the dependent variable vanish, so the usual gradient expression is undefined at exactly the member the question needs.
questions.question: For each real number $k$, the line $\ell_k$ has equation $(k + 2)x + (k - 1)y = 2k + 7$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that every line $\ell_k$ passes through a single fixed point $P$, and state the coordinates of $P$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the value of $k$ for which $\ell_k$ is perpendicular to the line joining $P$ to the origin, giving your answer in the form $ax + by = c$ with integers $a$, $b$, $c$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the value of $k$ for which $\ell_k$ is parallel to the $y$-axis, and explain why the expression $-(k+2)/(k-1)$ for the gradient cannot be used to find it.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The line $\ell_k$ meets the coordinate axes at $A$ and $B$; show that the area of triangle $OAB$ is $\frac{(2k+7)^2}{2|(k+2)(k-1)|}$, and hence find the value of $k$ with $-2 < k < 1$ for which this area is exactly $6$.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Substituting $x = 3$ and $y = -1$ into the left-hand side gives $(k+2)(3) + (k-1)(-1) = 3k + 6 - k + 1 = 2k + 7$. **(M1)** This equals the right-hand side for every value of $k$, so $(3, -1)$ lies on every line of the family. **(A1)** Hence the fixed point is $P = (3, -1)$. **(A1)(R1)**

**(b)** The gradient of $PO$ is $(-1 - 0)/(3 - 0) = -1/3$. **(M1)** A line perpendicular to $PO$ therefore has gradient $3$. **(A1)** The gradient of $\ell_k$ is $-(k+2)/(k-1)$, so $-(k+2)/(k-1) = 3$. **(M1)** This gives $-k - 2 = 3k - 3$, so $k = 1/4$. **(A1)** Substituting, $\ell_{1/4}$ is $(9/4)x - (3/4)y = 15/2$, which simplifies to $3x - y = 10$. **(AG)**

**(c)** When $k = 1$ the equation becomes $3x + 0y = 9$, that is $x = 3$, a vertical line parallel to the $y$-axis. **(A1)** The expression $-(k+2)/(k-1)$ was obtained by dividing by the coefficient of $y$, namely $k - 1$. **(R1)** At $k = 1$ that coefficient is zero, so the division is not defined. **(R1)** The formula therefore does not apply, and the vertical line must be read directly from the equation. **(A1)**

**(d)** The $x$-intercept is $A = ((2k+7)/(k+2), 0)$ and the $y$-intercept is $B = (0, (2k+7)/(k-1))$. **(M1)** The area of triangle $OAB$ is $\frac{1}{2}\left|\frac{2k+7}{k+2}\right|\left|\frac{2k+7}{k-1}\right| = \frac{(2k+7)^2}{2|(k+2)(k-1)|}$. **(A1)** Setting this equal to $6$ and using that $(k+2)(k-1) < 0$ on $-2 < k < 1$ gives $(2k+7)^2 = -12(k+2)(k-1)$. **(M1)** Expanding, $4k^2 + 28k + 49 = -12k^2 - 12k + 24$, so $16k^2 + 40k + 25 = 0$. **(A1)** This is $(4k+5)^2 = 0$, so $k = -5/4$. **(A1)** Then $\ell_{-5/4}$ is $x - 3y = 6$, with intercepts $6$ and $-2$, and the area is $\frac{1}{2}(6)(2) = 6$. **(R1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: Part (a) awards **(M1)** for substituting $(3, -1)$ and **(A1)** for verifying that the identity holds for all $k$, with a second **(A1)** for stating $P = (3, -1)$; the **(R1)** recognises the alternative grouping $k(x+y-2) + (2x-y-7) = 0$. A candidate who finds $P$ by solving two particular members earns the same credit. In part (b) the **(M1)** is for the gradient $-1/3$ of $PO$ and the **(A1)** for the perpendicular gradient $3$; the second **(M1)** is for solving $-(k+2)/(k-1) = 3$ and the **(A1)** for $k = 1/4$, with the **(AG)** confirming $3x - y = 10$. In part (c) the **(A1)** is for identifying $k = 1$ and the vertical line $x = 3$, while the two **(R1)** marks are for the observation that the formula divides by $k - 1$ and that this coefficient is zero at $k = 1$; the final **(A1)** states the conclusion. Part (d) awards **(M1)** for the two intercepts and **(A1)** for the area expression. The **(M1)** is for using $(k+2)(k-1) < 0$ on the given interval to remove the modulus with a sign change, and the **(A1)** marks are for the quadratic $16k^2 + 40k + 25 = 0$ and for the double root $k = -5/4$; the **(R1)** is for the numerical check that the area is $6$.
questions.explanation:
The family of lines is controlled by one parameter, and the whole item is organised around the single value $k = 1$ at which the usual description of the line breaks down. Part (a) is a fixed-point argument: because the coefficients of $k$ can be collected, every member passes through the point where $x + y - 2 = 0$ and $2x - y - 7 = 0$ meet, and that point is $P = (3, -1)$. Recognising the family as a pencil through a fixed point is the organising idea for the rest of the question.

Parts (b) and (c) sit on either side of the degeneracy. For part (b) the gradient formula $-(k+2)/(k-1)$ is valid, because $k = 1/4$ keeps the coefficient of $y$ away from zero, and the perpendicularity condition reduces to a linear equation. Part (c) asks for the one member that the formula cannot see: at $k = 1$ the coefficient of $y$ is zero, the line is vertical, and the division that produced the gradient is undefined. The candidate has to abandon the formula and read the vertical line directly from the equation.

Part (d) adds the area of the triangle cut off by the axes. The modulus is essential, but on the interval $-2 < k < 1$ the product $(k+2)(k-1)$ is negative, so removing the modulus reverses a sign and produces the perfect square $(4k+5)^2 = 0$. The double root is a feature, not an accident: the area function is tangent to the level $6$ at that parameter value, so the condition has exactly one solution in the interval. The fixed point found in part (a) is what ties the three later parts together, because every geometric statement about $\ell_k$ can be translated into an equation involving $k$ and that common point.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 2.1 bullet on the different forms of the equation of a straight line and the SL 2.4 bullet on determining key features of graphs. The design puts the failure inside the family itself: at exactly one parameter value the coefficient of the dependent variable vanishes, so the usual gradient expression is undefined precisely at the member the question needs. The family (k+2)x + (k-1)y = 2k + 7, the fixed point (3, -1), the perpendicular member 3x - y = 10, the vertical member x = 3, and the area condition that collapses to the perfect square (4k+5)^2 = 0 at k = -5/4 are all constructed here.

verification.method: The fixed point was tested against four parameter values, the perpendicular member and its intercepts were recomputed, and the area equation and its double root were confirmed by direct substitution.

questions.title: A composite function that loses one point and one value
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 2.2 (concept of a function, domain, range and graph) and SL 2.3 (the graph of a function; its equation y = f(x))
questions.subtopic: 2.2 Concept of a function, domain, range and graph and 2.3 The graph of a function
questions.challenge_mechanism: The lever is that the algebraic cancellation removes a factor whose zero is a real input, so a single deleted input survives as a single missing value in the range.
questions.question: The functions $f$ and $g$ are defined by $f(x) = \sqrt{x + 5}$ and $g(x) = \frac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the largest possible domain of $f$ and the corresponding range of $f$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the inverse function $f^{-1}$, stating its domain and its range.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the largest possible domain of the composite function $g \circ f$, and simplify $(g \circ f)(x)$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the range of $g \circ f$ is not the interval $[3, \infty)$, and state the value that is missing.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The expression $\sqrt{x+5}$ is defined when the radicand is non-negative, so $x + 5 \ge 0$, that is $x \ge -5$. **(A1)** The largest possible domain is therefore $[-5, \infty)$. **(A1)** The endpoint $-5$ is included because the radicand is exactly zero there. A square root takes only non-negative values, and as $x$ runs over the domain the value $\sqrt{x+5}$ covers every non-negative number, so the range is $[0, \infty)$. **(A1)**

**(b)** Setting $y = \sqrt{x+5}$ and squaring gives $y^2 = x + 5$, so $x = y^2 - 5$. **(M1)** Interchanging $x$ and $y$, $f^{-1}(x) = x^2 - 5$. **(A1)** The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$, namely $x \ge 0$. **(A1)** The range of $f^{-1}$ is the domain of $f$, namely $y \ge -5$. **(A1)**

**(c)** For $x$ in the domain of $f$, $(g \circ f)(x) = \frac{(f(x))^2 - 9}{f(x) - 3} = \frac{(f(x)-3)(f(x)+3)}{f(x)-3} = f(x) + 3 = \sqrt{x+5} + 3$. **(M1)** This simplification requires $f(x) \ne 3$. **(R1)** Now $\sqrt{x+5} = 3$ exactly when $x + 5 = 9$, that is $x = 4$. **(A1)** The value $x = 4$ lies in the domain of $f$ but must be removed from the domain of $g \circ f$. **(A1)** Hence the largest possible domain is $[-5, 4) \cup (4, \infty)$. **(A1)**

**(d)** As $x$ runs over $[-5, \infty)$, the expression $\sqrt{x+5} + 3$ takes every value from $3$ upwards, so the naive range is $[3, \infty)$. **(R1)** However, $x = 4$ has been excluded from the domain, and at $x = 4$ the composite would take the value $\sqrt{9} + 3 = 6$. **(A1)** That single value is therefore missing, and the range is $[3, 6) \cup (6, \infty)$. **(A1)** The value $6$ is approached as $x$ approaches $4$ from either side, so it is a single isolated gap rather than an interval of missing values.
questions.markscheme_notes: Part (a) awards three **(A1)** marks, one for the domain $x \ge -5$, one for writing it as $[-5, \infty)$, and one for the range $[0, \infty)$; the range mark requires the candidate to note that a square root is non-negative. In part (b) the **(M1)** is for squaring and rearranging to $x = y^2 - 5$, and the **(A1)** is for $f^{-1}(x) = x^2 - 5$. The remaining two **(A1)** marks are for the domain $x \ge 0$ and the range $y \ge -5$ of the inverse, which come from swapping the domain and range of $f$; a candidate who writes $x \ge -5$ for the inverse has not swapped them and loses that mark. Part (c) awards **(M1)** for the algebraic simplification to $\sqrt{x+5} + 3$ and **(R1)** for stating that this requires $f(x) \ne 3$. The **(A1)** marks are for solving $\sqrt{x+5} = 3$ to get $x = 4$, for recognising that $4$ lies in the domain of $f$ but not of the composite, and for the final domain $[-5, 4) \cup (4, \infty)$. Part (d) awards **(R1)** for the naive range $[3, \infty)$ and **(A1)** for the excluded value $6$; the final **(A1)** is for the range $[3, 6) \cup (6, \infty)$. A candidate who omits the missing value cannot earn the last two marks.
questions.explanation:
The two functions are individually simple, and the difficulty comes from the single point at which the composite loses meaning. Part (a) fixes the domain and range of $f$, and part (b) forces the candidate to remember that the inverse function exchanges them: the domain of $f^{-1}$ is $[0, \infty)$ and its range is $[-5, \infty)$, not the other way round. This swap is the standard trap, and it matters later because it determines which values the composite can produce.

Part (c) is the core of the item. The quotient $((f(x))^2 - 9)/(f(x) - 3)$ simplifies to $f(x) + 3$ only where $f(x) \ne 3$, and $f(x) = 3$ precisely at $x = 4$. The cancellation is legitimate algebra but it removes a genuine hole, so the largest domain of $g \circ f$ is $[-5, \infty)$ with $4$ deleted. A candidate who cancels without recording the exclusion has quietly changed the function.

Part (d) makes that hole visible. The simplified expression $\sqrt{x+5} + 3$ would sweep out $[3, \infty)$, but the excluded input $x = 4$ would have produced exactly $6$, so $6$ alone is missing. The range is therefore $[3, 6) \cup (6, \infty)$. This is the point of the question: an algebraic simplification can hide a single deleted value, and only tracking the domain reveals it. A second subtlety is that the domain of the composite is not the whole domain of $f$: because $g$ is undefined at its own denominator zero, the input that makes $f(x) = 3$ must be removed, and this removal is invisible once the fraction has been cancelled. Candidates who work only with the simplified expression $\sqrt{x+5} + 3$ will state a range that is too large. Checking a value just below and just above $x = 4$ confirms that the composite approaches $6$ from both sides but never attains it.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 2.2 bullet on the concept of a function, domain and range and the SL 2.3 bullet on the graph of a function. The design makes the algebraic cancellation remove a factor whose zero is a genuine input, so one deleted input survives as a single missing value in the range. The functions sqrt(x+5) and (x^2-9)/(x-3), the composite sqrt(x+5)+3, the excluded input x = 4 and the resulting gap at the value 6, together with the domain-and-range swap in the inverse, are all constructed here.

verification.method: The domain and range endpoints were evaluated directly, the inverse was checked at three inputs, and the composite and the excluded value were confirmed numerically at sample points.

questions.title: The zeros and the poles swap places
questions.subject: Math AA HL
questions.syllabus_ref: SL 2.4 (determining key features of graphs) and SL 2.8 (the reciprocal function f(x) = 1/x)
questions.subtopic: 2.4 Key features of graphs and 2.8 The reciprocal function
questions.challenge_mechanism: The lever is that taking the reciprocal interchanges the zeros and the vertical asymptotes, and the resulting inequality then depends on which critical values are poles rather than roots.
questions.question: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x) = \frac{2x + 3}{x - 1}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the equations of the asymptotes and the coordinates of the intercepts of the graph of $y = f(x)$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find an expression for $\frac{1}{f(x)}$ in the form $\frac{x+a}{bx+c}$, and state the equations of its asymptotes and the coordinates of its intercepts.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the asymptotes and intercepts of $y = \frac{1}{f(x)}$ relate to those of $y = f(x)$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Solve the inequality $f(x) \ge \frac{1}{f(x)}$, giving your answer in interval notation.

questions.answer:
**(a)** A vertical asymptote occurs where the denominator vanishes, so $x - 1 = 0$ gives $x = 1$. **(A1)** The function is undefined there, so $x = 1$ is excluded from the domain. Dividing, $\frac{2x+3}{x-1} = 2 + \frac{5}{x-1}$, so as $x \to \pm\infty$ the graph approaches $y = 2$; this is the horizontal asymptote. **(A1)** The $y$-intercept is $f(0) = 3/(-1) = -3$, giving $(0, -3)$. **(A1)** The $x$-intercept solves $2x + 3 = 0$, so $x = -3/2$, giving $(-3/2, 0)$. **(A1)**

**(b)** Taking the reciprocal, $\frac{1}{f(x)} = \frac{x-1}{2x+3}$. **(M1)** This has the form $\frac{x+a}{bx+c}$ with $a = -1$, $b = 2$, $c = 3$. **(A1)** Its vertical asymptote is $x = -3/2$, where the denominator vanishes, and its horizontal asymptote is $y = 1/2$, the ratio of the leading coefficients. **(A1)** The $y$-intercept is $(0, -1/3)$ and the $x$-intercept is $(1, 0)$. **(A1)**

**(c)** The $x$-intercept of $f$ at $x = -3/2$ becomes the vertical asymptote of $1/f$, and the vertical asymptote of $f$ at $x = 1$ becomes the $x$-intercept of $1/f$; in other words, the zeros and the poles swap roles. **(R1)** The horizontal asymptote changes from $y = 2$ to its reciprocal $y = 1/2$. **(R1)** The $y$-intercept changes from $-3$ to its reciprocal $-1/3$, since $1/f(0) = 1/(-3)$. **(R1)**

**(d)** The inequality is $\frac{2x+3}{x-1} \ge \frac{x-1}{2x+3}$. **(M1)** Subtracting the right-hand side and combining over the common denominator $(x-1)(2x+3)$ gives $\frac{(2x+3)^2 - (x-1)^2}{(x-1)(2x+3)} \ge 0$. **(M1)** The numerator factorises as $\left[(2x+3) - (x-1)\right]\left[(2x+3) + (x-1)\right] = (x+4)(3x+2)$. **(A1)** So the inequality is $\frac{(x+4)(3x+2)}{(x-1)(2x+3)} \ge 0$. **(A1)** The critical values are $-4$, $-3/2$, $-2/3$ and $1$, and a sign table gives the solution $(-\infty, -4] \cup (-3/2, -2/3] \cup (1, \infty)$; the endpoints $-4$ and $-2/3$ are included because the numerator vanishes there, while $-3/2$ and $1$ are excluded because the expression is undefined there. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes: Part (a) awards **(A1)** for the vertical asymptote $x = 1$, **(A1)** for the horizontal asymptote $y = 2$, and **(A1)** for each intercept, giving $(0, -3)$ and $(-3/2, 0)$. Writing the function as $2 + 5/(x-1)$ is the cleanest route to the horizontal asymptote and should be credited. In part (b) the **(M1)** is for taking the reciprocal, and the **(A1)** marks are for the form $(x-1)/(2x+3)$, the two asymptotes $x = -3/2$ and $y = 1/2$, and the two intercepts $(0, -1/3)$ and $(1, 0)$; a candidate who inverts only the numerator or only the denominator earns nothing. Part (c) awards three **(R1)** marks, one for the interchange of zeros and poles, one for the horizontal asymptote becoming the reciprocal $1/2$, and one for the $y$-intercept becoming $-1/3$. In part (d) the **(M1)** marks are for writing the inequality with a common denominator and for expanding $(2x+3)^2 - (x-1)^2$, and the **(A1)** is for the factorisation $(x+4)(3x+2)$; the final two **(A1)** marks are for the correct critical values and the interval solution. Endpoint inclusion is essential: $-4$ and $-2/3$ are included because the numerator vanishes, while $-3/2$ and $1$ are excluded because the expression is undefined. The two excluded endpoints must be written with open brackets, since the expression is not defined there.
questions.explanation:
Reciprocating a function rearranges its graph in a very specific way, and the item is designed so that this rearrangement is the object of study rather than a by-product. In part (a) the rational function is read for its asymptotes and intercepts; rewriting it as $2 + 5/(x-1)$ makes the horizontal asymptote immediate and shows that the graph is a shifted hyperbola.

Part (b) asks for $1/f$ explicitly, and the key observation is that the reciprocal of a rational function is obtained by swapping numerator and denominator. The consequence is a complete exchange of roles: the zero of $f$ at $x = -3/2$ becomes the pole of $1/f$, and the pole of $f$ at $x = 1$ becomes the zero of $1/f$. The horizontal asymptote changes to the reciprocal of the original one, and the $y$-intercept changes to the reciprocal of the original intercept. Part (c) asks the candidate to state this pattern, which is where the structural understanding is assessed.

Part (d) turns the comparison $f(x) \ge 1/f(x)$ into a rational inequality. Collecting terms over the common denominator $(x-1)(2x+3)$ produces a difference of two squares, which factorises into a product of two linear factors over a product of two linear factors. The four critical values split the line into five intervals, and a sign table decides each one. The subtlety is endpoint behaviour: where the numerator vanishes the inequality is satisfied, but where the denominator vanishes it is undefined, so two endpoints are included and two are excluded. The comparison also shows why the horizontal asymptotes are reciprocals rather than equal: the behaviour at large $x$ of $1/f$ is the reciprocal of the behaviour of $f$, so $y = 2$ becomes $y = 1/2$, while the two finite critical values simply exchange their roles as roots and poles.

provenance.adaptation: Built from the SL 2.4 bullet on determining key features of graphs and the SL 2.8 bullet on the reciprocal function. The design uses reciprocity as the lever: taking 1/f interchanges the zeros and the vertical asymptotes, so the inequality that follows depends on which critical values are poles rather than roots. The function (2x+3)/(x-1), its asymptotes x = 1 and y = 2, the reciprocal (x-1)/(2x+3), the four critical values -4, -3/2, -2/3 and 1, and the final solution set are all constructed here.

verification.method: The asymptotes and intercepts of both functions were evaluated numerically, the numerator factorisation was tested at the critical values, and the sign of the inequality was checked at sample points in every interval.
